newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity settles sharply higher with cash.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity settles sharply higher with cash.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures settled sharply higher Tuesday, taking cue from stronger cash market prices tied to the current slate of plant outages and firm air-conditioning demand in the Southwest.
May California-Oregon Border (COB) futures ended up 68 cents at $14.11 a megawatt hour (MWh), trimming a $1.27 gain. June COB finished up 21 cents at $13.08. Other COB settled 13 to 20 cents higher.
May Palo Verde (PV) ended up $1.40 at $18.88, near its session high of $18.90. June PV finished up 81 cents at $19.26. Deferred PV months settled up 45 cents to $1.60.

The power complex managed to finish with substantial gains after an early rally fizzled. The morning jump was triggered by concerns over an operating problem at the 1,221 megawatt (MW) Palo Verde nuclear unit 2 near Page, Arizona. The rise faded midday when the plant's operator reported the problem did not affect Palo Verde 2's electricity production.
Main Southwest cities like Albuquerque, Los Angeles and Phoenix would see peak temperatures in the 70s-80s tomorrow and in the 60s-70s by Friday, forecasters said.
Day-ahead firm, peak power prices at COB rose $1-2 to $18.50-19.50, while those at PV jumped $2-3 to $22.00-25.00.
Brokers and traders said cash prices were also bolstered when Bonneville Power Administration withheld offers to sell next-day peak electricity.
"Once it didn't happen, prices went up," said one Houston futures trader.

Monday's return of BPA in the western spot market after disappearing for more than a week pushed cash power values lower. Many participants were somewhat surprised by BPA's retreat today, market sources said.
Some market sources said stronger spot natural gas prices at the Southwest also helped propel cash power prices higher.
Northwest Pipeline said its Chehalis gas compressor station will be shut tomorrow for about two weeks for repairs.

The outage of Chehalis facility in southwestern Washington is expected to cut gas flow on the Northwest Pipeline from Canada to the western U.S. by 130 million cubic feet per day. The unplanned shutdown forced some Southwest utilities to procure gas supplies in the open market, market sources said.
Almost 7,500 MW of thermal generating capacity in the West are currently offline due to repairs, maintenance and hydropower displacement sales.

Moreover, three large nuclear power units in the West are shut for refueling and maintenance: the 1,087 MW Diablo Canyon nuclear unit 1 in Avila Beach, Calif.; the 1,080 MW San Onofre 3 nuclear power unit in San Clemente, Calif.; and the 1,158 MW WNP-2 nuclear plant in Richland, Washington.
NYMEX estimated 533 COB and 758 PV contracts were sold, up from yesterday's 447 COB and 466 PV lots.
